newsitem.title: USA: Christopher aims to shore up alliance against Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Christopher aims to shore up alliance against Iraq.

text.p: Secretary of State Warren Christopher's long-planned trip to Europe, which begins on Wednesday, has become an effort to shore up the coalition against Iraq after U.S. military action drew tepid support.

Six weeks ago, Christopher set visits this week to London, Paris and Bonn to "touch base" with key allies on issues that Britain, France and Germany must grapple with in the next few months, including Bosnia, NATO, Russia and the Middle East, spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
But because Iraqi President Saddam Hussein undertook a "military gambit" against rebel Kurds, "the issue of northern Iraq now becomes a major issue for the trip," Burns said.

In all three capitals, there will be "very detailed discussions about what we can continue to do together to implement the no-fly zones (over Iraq), to maintain Operation Provide Comfort (the Turkey-based multinational air operation that has deterred Iraqi attacks on civilians), and to maintain the very core international pressure that currently exists to condemn Saddam Hussein and to try to beat him back to withdraw his troops," Burns said.

The United States pounded Iraq on Tuesday with 27 cruise missiles in retaliation for Baghdad's capture of a rebel Kurdish city. Washington defended its action as a deterrent to Iraqi aggression against its own people and its neighbors.

But there was a lukewarm response from U.S. allies and friends. Only Washington's closest friends -- Britain, Germany, Japan and Canada -- backed the strikes, which followed an Iraqi military push into the Western-protected Kurdish area of northern Iraq.

France, which joins the United States and Britain in patrolling no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq, voiced concern. Spain, Italy and Turkey withheld their approval, while Russia was very critical.
Many experts read the reaction as evidence that time has eroded the U.S.-led international coalition that drove Iraq's forces out of Kuwait in 1991.
Burns insisted that the coalition against Saddam "remains intact" and that U.S. officials privately were receiving more support from coalition members than public statements suggested.

Christopher, who leaves Washington on Wednesday morning, flies first to London, where he meets on Thursday with British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind, then flies to Paris for talks with French President Jacques Chirac and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

He spends the night in Bonn ahead of talks on Friday with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and a speech in Stuttgart being billed as a major address on European security. He is to have dinner that evening with Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel.
On Saturday he flies back to London for lunch with British opposition leaders and has breakfast there on Sunday with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on the threatened Middle East peace process.

Christopher, who last met Levy in Israel in June, will stress "our very strong hopes that Israel and the Palestinians can continue to make progress in the (peace) talks that are currently under way (and that Syria and Lebanon) will continue to be open to the possibility of moving forward on Middle East peace process issues," Burns said.

Among other issues on Christopher's agenda are NATO, about whose enlargement the alliance is to take key decisions in December, and Bosnia, where planned Sept. 14 national elections will have a crucial impact on the size of troops the allies may have to leave in the country after December.

Christopher also expects to discuss Russia, where the health of President Boris Yeltsin has become an increasing concern, and U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whom Washington has vowed to oppose for a second four-year term.
